newsitem.title: UK: UK denies shifting stance on Lockerbie suspects.
newsitem.headline: UK denies shifting stance on Lockerbie suspects.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday denied it was considering new ways to end an impasse over the extradition of two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over the Scottish town of Lockerbie in 1988.
"There has been no change in policy," a foreign ministry spokesman said in response to an article in the Times newspaper which said the government was reconsidering its approach.

Two alleged Libyan intelligence agents have been indicted in both Britain and the United States on charges of planting explosives on board Pan Am 103 but Tripoli is refusing to hand them over. The explosion killed 270 people.

London and Washington want the two to be tried in either Scotland or the United States and have ruled out Libya's proposal that they be tried by Scottish judges under Scottish laws in a neutral country.

"The two must be put on trial in Scotland or the United States," the spokesman insisted by telephone, saying various newspapers had mistakenly reported that Prime Minister Tony Blair felt "uneasy" about the case.
"(Blair spokesman Alistair) Campbell in fact said the prime minister was concerned at the continuing impasse," the spokesman said.
"He is not concerned about the legal case against the Libyans. The Lord Advocate (Scotland's senior legal officer) is satisfied that the case against the Libyans is good."
In July the United Nations Security Council retained strict sanctions against Libya which were imposed in 1992 when it became clear Tripoli would not hand over the suspects.
